items.title: Will AI make life less meaningful? A survey finds optimism hinges on whether humans keep control.
items.summary: OpenAI recently announced that its latest artificial intelligence model had solved, in a matter of weeks, more than 100 math problems that humans had worked on for years. The news sparked what seemed like an existential crisis among mathematicians, leaving some to wonder what role humans would have in the future of their field. It’s not just academics who are worried. In a new national survey , we found that Americans are more likely to see AI as a threat to meaning than as a resource that supports it. But that view depends on whether people think of AI as a tool that will remain under human control or as something that will become autonomous. Discussions about AI tend to focus on its practical costs and benefits, from job loss and cyberattacks to scientific and medical breakthroughs. Far less attention has been paid to its potential psychological effects, especially on our sense of meaning. Humans are a distinctly existential species. We don’t just strive for survival but also for significance, and people who perceive their lives as meaningful tend to be more psychologically healthy and resilient. A strong sense of meaning also promotes physical health and longevity, goal achievement, financial success, and prosocial behavior. This is because meaning is ultimately a self-regulatory and motivational resource. When we believe our lives matter, we have a reason to make the daily decisions and pursue the long-term ambitions that keep us healthy, productive, and connected to others. Much of what makes life meaningful comes from our relationships, work, and creative pursuits. AI is increasingly involved in all of these human endeavors. It writes code, creates art, and solves complex intellectual problems. People are even turning to it for the kind of conversation and counsel they once sought from other humans. As AI takes on a bigger role in these parts of life, how will it affect our sense of meaning? Others, including some of the people building AI, believe it is a fundamentally different technology — one on a path to becoming self-directed or autonomous. As part of a new research initiative on AI and the good life, our team at the Archbridge Institute’s Human Flourishing Lab surveyed over 2,000 Americans to explore this question. Specifically, we presented them with two views on how AI will affect meaning and asked which one they agree with most. In one, AI supports meaning by helping individuals put more of themselves into their relationships, work, and other purpose-driven pursuits. In the other, AI undermines meaning by doing more of people’s thinking and deciding for them, leading them to put less of themselves into these pursuits. In other words, we wanted to determine whether Americans are more inclined to view AI as supporting or undermining human meaning-making. Americans are more likely to view AI as undermining meaning (56%) than supporting it (44%). Women and older adults were especially likely to hold this view of AI as a threat to meaning. Meanwhile, men and younger Americans were more evenly divided. We also suspected that people’s attitudes about how AI will affect meaning would be connected to how they conceptualize AI. There is an active debate about what kind of technology AI is. Some think of it as a powerful but normal technology, like electricity or the internet, that will remain a tool humans direct and control. Others, including some of the people building AI, believe it is a fundamentally different technology — one on a path to becoming self-directed or autonomous. We asked Americans which view they agree with most, and they are almost evenly split. Forty-eight percent see AI as a normal, human-directed technology, while 52% see it as a fundamentally new technology that will become autonomous. Why would these views be connected to meaning? Ultimately, people find their lives most meaningful when they believe that they matter, that their efforts make a difference in the world. If people think of AI as a tool that humans control, like past technologies, they may view it as something that can help them make a difference, even if it disrupts how they live and work. But if they imagine it as fundamentally new because it could become autonomous, they may worry that humans will no longer be the primary agents in the world, making their contributions less significant As predicted, how people conceptualize AI is strongly related to how they think it will affect meaning. Among Americans who envision AI as human-directed, 63% believe it will support people’s ability to live meaningful lives, and 37% believe it will undermine it. Among those who expect AI to be autonomous, the pattern flips. Just 27% believe AI will support meaning, and 73% believe it will undermine it. This relationship held across every demographic group we examined, and it was larger than any of the demographic differences we observed. As we grapple with existential concerns about AI, it is worth remembering that technological innovation has always disrupted economic and cultural life, and it has likely challenged people’s sense of meaning along the way. But humans adapted. We are an agentic, creative, and resilient species. The same ingenuity that made AI possible can help us find new ways to make significant contributions to the world. And regardless of what this technology becomes, we will still decide how much of ourselves we put into the people, projects, and pursuits that make life meaningful. items.title: Memories of the Train
items.summary: Illustrations by Katherine Lam The train’s seats : blue with a white strip down the middle. The windows: wide, tinted green. The sun: halfway below the horizon. He was playing with the top his mother had bought from the cart lady. With each spin came flashes of rainbow light: zzz zzz zoom. The train’s seats: white with a blue strip down the middle, five per row. The windows: wide, tinted blue. A hard orange sunlight cut through the glass. He was playing with the top his mother had bought. Next to him was his brother, Dudu. Dudu was 4. He was 9. Their mother was in the bathroom. With each spin came flashes of rainbow light: zzz zzz zoom. The train’s seats: mostly blue and a little white, five per row. They sat in row 18. Earlier Dudu, giggling, had knocked over the top. Annoyed, he’d slapped Dudu’s hand away. Dudu had grown bored and fallen asleep. Their mother, before going to the bathroom, had told him to watch his little brother. Now the train pulled into a station, and he tried to read the name of it in the glare of the setting sun. He could recognize only two of the four characters: hill and city . Their stop was the next one, but as people got off the train, others were already standing up, reaching for their luggage. The top rolled from the tray table onto the floor, bounced, and slid under the rows in front of him. He crawled on the floor, dodging people’s shoes and thighs and suitcases, until he snatched it back into the safety of his small, warm fist. When he crawled back to his seat, Dudu was gone. The woman: same height as his mother. Hair in a bun. Dangling earrings. She held Dudu the way their mother held him. Dudu, whose head rested on her shoulder, opened his eyes drowsily as she carried him off the train. In an instant they were swarmed by bodies on the platform. Through the window he caught a glimpse of the woman’s face, which looked ordinary, which he’d later fail to describe with any specificity to the sketch artist at the police station. Over the woman’s shoulder, Dudu’s face pinched in confusion. Inside the train, he heard a wail, sharp and alarmed, coming from his own throat. His fist pounded the glass. But the train had already begun moving. After his brother was abducted on the train between Changsha and Guangzhou, his parents bankrupted themselves. They closed their convenience store. They camped outside the local police station. When the police moved on to other things, they spent all their money on an incompetent local detective. They spent all their time plastering ads on the telephone poles of a city that had been neither a home nor a destination. But Dudu remained gone. A few seasons passed before they finally returned to their run-down apartment in Changsha, but it felt like years. His mother’s hair had turned white. His father’s cheeks sagged permanently, as if they were trying to run away from the rest of his face. The room he had once shared with Dudu was frighteningly quiet at night without the sound of Dudu’s soft, wet snores. Back then he believed that the walkie-talkie his father had given him for his seventh birthday had magic powers. At night, he’d take the cold block in his hands and press it against his ear, whispering, “Dudu, Dudu, can you hear me? Come back, I need you for our mission. Over.” Silence spread through the house and wrapped everyone in their own impenetrable cocoon. He knew that his mother blamed him for what had happened, though she never said it aloud, and though he’d told the police that on the train he’d begun screaming and pounding the window right away to get the other passengers’ attention. Some mornings, in the apartment’s heavy stillness, his mother set down boiled eggs in front of him without cooling them in water. They blistered his fingers when he tried to peel them. He knew that she did it on purpose—she used to always cool them for him first. He knew that his father, though he never said it aloud, blamed his mother for what had happened. His father had once swept the hair that his mother would shed in the bathroom without complaint. Now he hardly spent time in the apartment at all. His mother’s white strands piled around the toilet like a thin layer of frost. When his parents divorced, he chose to live with his father, because his father intended to go as far away as possible, while his mother intended on staying. She was convinced that Dudu would one day find his way back to their crumbling apartment. He followed his father to a new city, then another new city, then another new city. He toted around the shoebox that held the top and the walkie-talkie with each move. He hid the fact that he had a brother from each new friend he made, each time he introduced himself to a class. During those years, he tried to forget about what had happened. But once in a while, he’d visit his mother and see that she continued to sit in a dark corner of their old apartment, shedding hair, shelling peanuts, waiting for Dudu to knock on the door, waiting to die. The visit would dissolve any sense of movement in his own life. His mother continued to bake cakes on Dudu’s birthday. She told him she worried that if Dudu called, she would no longer recognize his voice—surely puberty would have thickened his vocal cords, given him the tenor of a strange man. When his father moved to the United States, he went along. He gave himself a new name in the new country: Brent, which means “hill.” Brent made new friends who believed he was an only child. He was unable to tell the first two women he loved about what had happened. The third woman, after he told her, drew his head down onto her lap and stroked his hair until dawn. He married her. They lived happily together for six years and unhappily for two, then parted ways. He made a lot of money one year and lost it all the next. Both of his parents died. On their deathbeds, both of his parents spoke of Dudu and cried. Throughout the years, the only constant in his life was Dudu’s absence. So many of his nightmares started with the top. He blamed the top for what had happened almost as much as he blamed himself. If his mother hadn’t bought him the top, he and Dudu would have invented some game to play together. The games they once played included: “you be the soldier and I’ll be the general,” “you be the plane and I’ll be the captain,” “you be the rabbit and I’ll be the farmer,” “you be the fox and I’ll be the dog.” If they’d played a game, Dudu wouldn’t have fallen asleep. If he hadn’t been looking for the top, he wouldn’t have lost track of Dudu. If he’d been a kinder older brother, he would have let Dudu play with the top and Dudu wouldn’t have fallen asleep. If … The list went on. “Do you find yourself consumed by all the things that could have gone a different way?” his therapist asked him. By then, he was living alone in a large brownstone in Boston after divorcing his second wife, who, despite her duplicitous nature, had been benevolent during the divorce proceedings. She’d agreed to a slightly smaller alimony on the sole condition that he start therapy. “Do you find yourself going down a rabbit hole of imagining alternative realities? Do you find yourself shaking, crying, unable to breathe normally when you follow this train of thought?” “Yes,” he said, frowning at the word train . The therapist opened a drawer and pressed a cold, hard fruit into his hands. “When that happens, try sucking on a lemon.” She cut off the top of the lemon with a pair of scissors. He put his mouth on the fruit’s cool flesh. The sourness was so intense, it shot a ray of numbness all the way up his neck and into his skull.
